essays.prompt: Common App personal essay: choose one of 7 prompts (Tara chose: a topic, idea or concept you find so engaging that it makes you lose all track of time) (650 words, shared by every Common App school)

versions.text:
I have always been passionate about technology and computers. From a young age, I was fascinated by how apps work and how they can make people's lives easier. This passion has led me to many different experiences that have shaped who I am today.

In Grade 10, I built a bus-tracking app for my school. Many students had problems knowing when the school bus would arrive, so I decided to solve this problem using technology. I used Flutter and Firebase and learned a lot about GPS and databases. The app is now used by many students and parents.

I also created a Malayalam flashcard app called Akshara. It helps people learn Malayalam words and has been downloaded more than 2,000 times on the Play Store. Building this app taught me about user interface design and how to publish an app.

In addition, I am the lead of my school's robotics club. As a leader, I learned teamwork, communication and time management. Our team took part in a national robotics competition and we worked very hard to prepare.

In my IB Diploma, I take Computer Science HL, Mathematics AA HL and Physics HL. These subjects have taught me problem solving and critical thinking. My Computer Science Internal Assessment is also about building software for a real client.

Through all of these experiences, I have learned that I love solving problems and that technology can change the world. I have also learned the importance of hard work, perseverance and never giving up, even when things are difficult.

In the future, I want to study Computer Science at a top university and become a software engineer. I want to use my skills to build technology that helps people in India and around the world. I believe that my passion, dedication and experience make me a strong candidate, and I am excited for the next chapter of my journey.

At 2:07 a.m. on a school night in Grade 10, the map on my laptop showed Bus 4 floating in the Atlantic Ocean, somewhere off the coast of Ghana. It was supposed to be on Old Airport Road in Bengaluru.

For three months I had been building an app that told students at my school when their bus would reach their stop. I used Flutter and Firebase, and a cheap GPS module that our transport manager let me tape under the dashboard of one bus. The app worked in testing. On its first real morning, forty parents opened it and watched the bus vanish to latitude zero, longitude zero.

I learned that night that the GPS module sent empty readings whenever the bus went under the Hebbal flyover, and my code was treating "nothing" as the number zero. The fix was four lines. Finding it took until 4 a.m., a lot of print statements, and a moment where I nearly deleted the whole project.

This experience taught me a lot about debugging and about perseverance. It also taught me that users do not care how clever the code is; they care about whether the bus is coming.

After the bus app, I built other projects. I made Akshara, a Malayalam flashcard app that now has more than 2,000 downloads. I lead the robotics club, where we built a line-following robot for a national competition. In IB, I take Computer Science HL, Maths AA HL and Physics HL, and my Computer Science IA is a timetable tool for our school library.

Each of these projects taught me something new. Akshara taught me about design, the robotics club taught me about leadership, and IB taught me to manage my time.

I want to study Computer Science because I want to keep building things that people actually use. I am excited to learn from professors and classmates who are passionate about the same things, and I know that university will challenge me to grow as a programmer and as a person.

At 2:07 a.m. on a school night in Grade 10, the map on my laptop showed Bus 4 floating in the Atlantic Ocean, somewhere off the coast of Ghana. It was supposed to be on Old Airport Road in Bengaluru.

For three months I had been building an app to tell students at my school when their bus would reach their stop: Flutter, Firebase, and a cheap GPS module our transport manager let me tape under the dashboard of one bus. It worked in testing. On its first real morning, forty parents opened it and watched the bus vanish to latitude zero, longitude zero.

By 4 a.m. I had found the bug. Every time the bus passed under the Hebbal flyover, the module lost its signal and sent an empty reading, and my code quietly turned "nothing" into the number zero. The fix was four lines: if there is no reading, keep the last real one and say so. The next morning the app showed "Last seen 40 seconds ago, Hebbal" instead of an ocean, and nobody complained.

I have thought about those four lines more than anything else I have written. My code had not crashed. It had confidently told forty people something false, because I had never asked what it should do when it did not know.

I asked that question again a year later, sitting next to my grandmother in Kochi. Ammamma taught Malayalam in a government school for thirty-one years, and when my cousins in Dubai and Bengaluru stopped being able to read her letters, she started writing to them in English, slowly, with mistakes she hated. I built Akshara, a flashcard app for Malayalam script, partly so my cousins could read her again. I tested it on her first.

She held the phone at arm's length and pressed the speaker icon four times before anything happened. The buttons I had designed for my own thumbs were too small for hers. The app assumed the user already knew which letters were vowels. It assumed good eyesight, a fast connection, and patience with a loading spinner. None of those assumptions had felt like assumptions when I wrote them.

I rebuilt the first screen around her: bigger targets, audio that plays offline, a "show me again" button instead of a score. When Akshara passed 2,000 downloads, the review I screenshotted was not a five-star one. It was from a man in Thrissur who wrote that his mother, seventy-eight, was using it to teach his daughter in Toronto over video calls.

Leading our robotics club this year, I see the same pattern in other people's code. When our line-follower drives off the table, the first instinct in the room is to blame the sensor. I have started asking a less comfortable question first: what did we tell the robot to do when it could not see the line?

I want to study computer science because I want to get better at that question, at scale. I want to learn the theory that explains why systems fail quietly, and to spend four years among people who will find the empty readings in my thinking faster than I can. I still keep a screenshot of Bus 4 in the Atlantic on my desktop. It reminds me that most bugs are not in the code. They are in what the code assumes about the world, and about the people in it.

essays.prompt: CMU short answer: the most significant reason for your chosen area(s) of study (300 words)

versions.text:
Carnegie Mellon is one of the best universities in the world for Computer Science. The School of Computer Science is ranked number one and has world-class professors and research facilities. I want to study at CMU because it will give me the best education and opportunities in technology. Many famous computer scientists have studied or taught at CMU, and its graduates work at top companies like Google, Microsoft and Apple.

I am interested in many areas of computer science, including artificial intelligence, mobile app development, robotics and cybersecurity. CMU has strong programs in all of these areas. I also like that CMU has a collaborative culture and many student clubs where I can continue my interest in robotics and app development.

In my IB Diploma I take Computer Science HL, Mathematics AA HL and Physics HL, and I have built several apps, so I am ready for the challenging curriculum at CMU. I believe that I would fit in well at CMU because I am passionate, hardworking and love technology. Studying at CMU would help me achieve my dream of becoming a successful software engineer and making a difference in the world. I would be proud and excited to be part of the CMU community.

The most significant reason I want to study computer science is a bug that put my school bus in the Atlantic Ocean. My GPS code turned a missing reading into the number zero, and forty parents watched Bus 4 disappear. Since then I have been interested in a specific problem: how software behaves when it does not know something.

At Carnegie Mellon I would study this from two directions. In 15-122, Principles of Imperative Computation, I would learn to write contracts that make a program's assumptions explicit, which is exactly what my bus app was missing. Through the Human-Computer Interaction Institute, I would learn how to study users like my grandmother, who could not press the buttons I had designed for my own thumbs on my Malayalam flashcard app.

I am also interested in robotics, and I would like to join ScottyLabs to keep building tools that other students use.

CMU appeals to me because it treats computer science as both rigorous and human, and that combination is what I want.

The most significant reason I want to study computer science is a bug that put my school bus in the Atlantic Ocean. My GPS code turned a missing reading into the number zero, and on the app's first morning forty parents watched Bus 4 vanish to latitude zero, longitude zero. The fix took four lines. The lesson has taken two years: the worst failures I have caused were not crashes but confident answers to questions my code did not understand.

That is why I want a computer science education that takes assumptions seriously. In 15-122, Principles of Imperative Computation, I would learn to write contracts that state what a function expects and what it promises, the habit my bus app was missing. I want to follow that thread into 15-213, where I suspect I will find many more ways to be confidently wrong.

The other half of the problem is people. When I tested Akshara, my Malayalam flashcard app, on my grandmother, she pressed the speaker icon four times before anything happened. I fixed the buttons, but I did not have a method, only a grandmother. The Human-Computer Interaction Institute would give me that method, and the Language Technologies Institute works on the problem behind Akshara itself: languages like Malayalam, spoken by more than thirty-five million people, that most software still treats as an afterthought.

I want to study computer science where rigour and empathy are neighbouring buildings rather than separate worlds, and where I can keep asking the question my bus taught me: what should this system do when it does not know?

essays.prompt: Waterloo Admission Information Form (AIF): describe your programming and computing experience, and why the Computer Science co-op stream (300 words)

versions.text:
I have been coding for five years. I know Python, Java, Dart and some C++, and I enjoy learning new frameworks and tools in my free time. I have built several projects, including a bus-tracking app for my school using Flutter and Firebase, a Malayalam flashcard app called Akshara with over 2,000 downloads on the Google Play Store, and a library timetable tool for my IB Computer Science IA.

I also lead my school's robotics club, where we program Arduino-based robots in C++. In addition, I have completed online courses such as CS50 and a Coursera course on algorithms. I have participated in hackathons and coding competitions, including the Canadian Computing Competition in 2026. These experiences have helped me improve my problem-solving skills and taught me how to work under pressure and with a team.

I am very interested in Waterloo's co-op program because I want to gain real-world experience while studying. Waterloo is known as one of the best universities for Computer Science in Canada, and many of its graduates work at leading technology companies around the world. I believe that my experience in coding and my passion for computer science make me a good fit for the Waterloo Computer Science program.

The most-used code I have written is four lines long. It decides what my school's bus tracker shows when the GPS module under the dashboard loses signal under the Hebbal flyover: the last real position, marked "last seen 40 seconds ago", instead of latitude zero. I built the first version in Grade 10 with Flutter and Firebase; about 300 students and parents now open it each morning.

Akshara, my Malayalam flashcard app (2,000+ downloads), taught me a different kind of engineering. Offline audio meant compressing 600 clips to under 9 MB so the app would run on my grandmother's phone and on slow connections in Kerala. I rewrote the spaced-repetition scheduler twice after reading about the SM-2 algorithm and realising my own version punished users for mistakes.

In the robotics club, which I lead, I moved our Arduino code from one shared file into a GitHub repository with code review, which caught two motor-control bugs before our regional round. I scored 38/75 on the CCC Senior paper in February 2026; S4 is the problem I still think about, because I solved it two days after the contest ended.

Waterloo's co-op stream matters to me because every project above improved most when real users broke it. Six work terms would give me that feedback loop with stakes higher than a school bus.
